Name: Large Magellanic Cloud
Notes: Largest Milky Way satellite; home of the Tarantula Nebula and SN 1987A.

Name: Small Magellanic Cloud
Notes: Gas-rich dwarf irregular, tidally stretched by the LMC and the Milky Way.

Name: Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal
Notes: Closest known satellite galaxy, being torn apart into a stream that wraps around the Milky Way.

Name: Boötes I
Notes: Ultra-faint dwarf discovered in SDSS data (2006); one of the most dark-matter dominated systems known.

Name: Draco Dwarf
Notes: Very dark-matter dominated satellite.

Name: Ursa Minor Dwarf
Notes: One of the oldest stellar populations of any Milky Way satellite.

Name: Sculptor Dwarf
Notes: First dwarf spheroidal discovered (Shapley 1937).

Name: Sextans Dwarf
Notes: Very low surface brightness satellite found in 1990.

Name: Carina Dwarf
Notes: Shows several distinct episodes of star formation.

Name: Fornax Dwarf
Notes: Brightest Milky Way dwarf spheroidal; has six globular clusters of its own.

Name: Leo II
Notes: Distant Milky Way satellite.

Name: Leo I
Notes: Distant, fast-moving satellite seen right next to Regulus on the sky.

Name: Phoenix Dwarf
Notes: Transition-type dwarf on the edge of the Local Group.

Name: NGC 6822
Notes: Barred dwarf irregular with bright H II regions.

Name: NGC 185
Notes: Dwarf elliptical satellite of Andromeda.

Name: NGC 147
Notes: Dwarf elliptical satellite of Andromeda.

Name: IC 1613
Notes: Isolated dwarf irregular with very little dust.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Notes: Nearest large galaxy and the most massive member of the Local Group; will merge with the Milky Way in ~4.5 billion years.

Name: M32
Notes: Compact elliptical satellite of Andromeda.

Name: IC 10
Notes: The only starburst galaxy in the Local Group.

Name: Leo A
Notes: Isolated dwarf dominated by young stars.

Name: M110
Notes: Bright dwarf elliptical satellite of Andromeda.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Notes: Third-largest Local Group galaxy; hosts the giant H II region NGC 604.

Name: Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte
Notes: Isolated dwarf irregular on the outskirts of the Local Group.

Name: Sextans A
Notes: Square-looking dwarf just beyond the Local Group.

Name: NGC 300
Notes: Face-on spiral in the Sculptor Group.

Name: IC 342
Notes: The "Hidden Galaxy": a large spiral dimmed by Milky Way dust.

Name: Maffei 1
Notes: Giant elliptical behind the Milky Way plane; only found in 1968 (infrared).

Name: NGC 253
Notes: Bright starburst spiral; the dominant member of the Sculptor Group.

Name: M82
Notes: Prototype starburst galaxy with a galactic superwind; tidally disturbed by M81.

Name: M81
Notes: Grand-design spiral at the heart of the M81 Group.

Name: Centaurus A
Notes: Nearest radio galaxy: a merger remnant with a dust lane, a 55 million M☉ black hole and kiloparsec jets.

Name: Circinus Galaxy
Notes: Nearby Seyfert 2 galaxy hidden behind the Galactic plane.

Name: M83
Notes: Barred grand-design spiral with a high supernova rate.

Name: M64
Notes: Dark dust band in front of its bright nucleus; outer gas counter-rotates.

Name: M101
Notes: Large face-on spiral; host of SN 2011fe.

Name: M106
Notes: Its nuclear water maser gives a geometric distance used to anchor the cosmic distance ladder.

Name: M51
Notes: Classic grand-design spiral interacting with its companion NGC 5195.

Name: Sombrero Galaxy
Notes: Bright bulge, prominent dust lane and a billion-solar-mass central black hole.

Name: M74
Notes: Face-on grand-design spiral, imaged by JWST in 2022.

Name: M87
Notes: Giant elliptical at the centre of the Virgo Cluster; its 6.5 billion M☉ black hole was the first ever imaged (2019).

Name: NGC 1300
Notes: Textbook barred spiral galaxy.

Name: Fornax Cluster
Notes: Richest nearby cluster after Virgo; centred on the giant elliptical NGC 1399.

Name: Antennae Galaxies
Notes: Pair of colliding galaxies with long tidal tails and intense star formation.

Name: Norma Cluster
Notes: Massive cluster near the centre of the Great Attractor, partly hidden by the Milky Way.

Name: Perseus Cluster
Notes: Brightest X-ray cluster in the sky; centred on the active galaxy NGC 1275 (Perseus A).

Name: Stephan's Quintet
Notes: First compact galaxy group discovered (1877); NGC 7320 in front of it is only ~13 Mpc away.

Name: Coma Cluster
Notes: Rich cluster of over 1,000 galaxies; where Zwicky first inferred dark matter (1933).

Name: Cartwheel Galaxy
Notes: Ring galaxy formed when a smaller galaxy plunged through its disc.

Name: Hoag's Object
Notes: Nearly perfect ring of young blue stars around an old yellow core.

Name: Cygnus A
Notes: One of the strongest radio sources in the sky; its lobes span ~140 kpc.

Name: 3C 273
Notes: First quasar identified (1963) and the optically brightest; its light left 2.0 billion years ago.
